quote: Against the assault of laughter nothing can stand.
source: Mark Twain, The Mysterious Stranger, ch. 10 (Satan) (Harper and Brothers, 1916)
speaker: Satan

evidence.where: Chapter 10 of the 1916 text as carried by Wikisource, Online Literature and American Literature, and the WIST quotation entry, all read this run; WIST also records the same passage in Twain's own manuscript
evidence.edition: The Mysterious Stranger, Harper and Brothers, 1916, the Paine and Duneka text
evidence.locator: ch. 10, in Satan's speech on the one effective weapon

reason: The sentence closes Satan's speech to the boys in chapter 10: For your race, in its poverty, has unquestionably one really effective weapon, laughter. Power, money, persuasion, supplication, persecution, these can lift at a colossal humbug, push it a little, weaken it a little, century by century; but only laughter can blow it to rags and atoms at a blast. Against the assault of laughter nothing can stand. The wording is exact, with no comma after laughter, and the speaker is Satan, so the source names him. The 1916 book was assembled after Twain's death by Albert Bigelow Paine and Frederick Duneka, which makes some of it unsafe to quote as Twain, but not this: the same passage stands in his own manuscript, The Chronicle of Young Satan, ch. 10, where only a neighbouring phrase differs, crowd it a little for push it a little. Note for the editor that three other July candidates are also Twain and only one person may stand in a month.
